name: Mitochondrial DNA Depletion Syndrome

criteria.description: Severe reduction in mitochondrial DNA copy number in affected tissues
Progressive multi-organ dysfunction including myopathy, hepatopathy, and encephalopathy
Identification of pathogenic mutations in nuclear genes involved in mtDNA maintenance (e.g., POLG, TK2, RRM2B)
Histological evidence of mitochondrial abnormalities such as ragged-red fibers or cytochrome c oxidase deficiency

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of severe mtDNA depletion in tissue plus compatible clinical presentation and pathogenic nuclear gene mutation
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis often requires integration of clinical, histological, biochemical, and genetic data.

common.symptomName: Linear arrays of macular hyperkeratoses in flexural areas

laboratory: Elevated lactate and pyruvate levels in blood and CSF
imaging: Brain MRI showing cerebral atrophy or basal ganglia abnormalities
other: Muscle biopsy showing ragged-red fibers and cytochrome c oxidase deficiency

distinguishingFeatures: Characteristic symmetric lesions in basal ganglia and brainstem on MRI
Usually caused by mitochondrial respiratory chain defects without mtDNA depletion
Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with pigmentary retinopathy
Large-scale mtDNA deletions rather than depletion

redFlags: Rapidly progressive muscle weakness and hypotonia in infancy
Severe lactic acidosis refractory to treatment
Multi-organ failure including liver and neurological deterioration
references: El-Hattab AW, Scaglia F. Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes: review and updates of genetic basis, manifestations, and therapeutic options. Neurotherapeutics. 2013;10(2):186-198.
Spinazzola A, Zeviani M. Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes. In: GeneReviews® [Internet]. University of Washington, Seattle; 2006.
Rahman S, Copeland WC. POLG-related disorders and their neurological manifestations. Nat Rev Neurol. 2019;15(1):40-52.
commonPitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as primary mitochondrial myopathies without genetic testing.
Symptoms may be attributed to more common neuromuscular disorders such as muscular dystrophies.
Liver involvement may be mistaken for other causes of hepatic failure in infants.
Overlooked in cases presenting with isolated myopathy or encephalopathy without multi-system involvement.

extendedDiscriminators.feature: Mitochondrial DNA Depletion Syndrome typically presents with severe myopathy and/or liver failure, whereas Leigh syndrome is characterized by subacute necrotizing encephalopathy with prominent brainstem and basal ganglia involvement on MRI.

Kearns-Sayre syndrome presents with progressive external ophthalmoplegia and pigmentary retinopathy, while Mitochondrial DNA Depletion Syndrome usually lacks these features and instead shows early-onset myopathy or hepatopathy.

Mitochondrial DNA Depletion Syndrome is distinguished by evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction (e.g., lactic acidosis, ragged red fibers on muscle biopsy) and confirmed by reduced mtDNA copy number, which are absent in typical muscular dystrophies.

ruleOutCriteria: Normal mitochondrial DNA copy number in affected tissue excludes Mitochondrial DNA Depletion Syndrome.
Absence of clinical or laboratory evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction (e.g., no lactic acidosis, normal muscle biopsy) essentially rules out the diagnosis.
